name: Grace Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't campaign for anything. It's all confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a breaking news and video reporter for a commercial regional news site, the kind that lives on adverts and app downloads. I start at seven with the police and fire service alerts, and I use AI every day: it drafts the first version of a crash or road-closure story from the official alert, and I check it and add what I've seen. Most days I'm out in the car with a phone and a small microphone, filming at a flood, a fire or a planning protest. In the evenings I write my own paid newsletter about the valley where I grew up, which brings in about three hundred a month.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love being first on the scene and getting it right, and I love that my newsletter readers email me like I'm their neighbour, because often I am. What wears me down is the late shifts and the comment sections, which can be vicious. I live with my partner Luke, who runs a small landscaping business, and between us we've got about three months of money saved. We go to church most Sundays, and that's where half my best tips come from, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Okay. Then I've just got some quite good tools and that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful, nothing magic, and that the people who panicked wasted a lot of energy. I'd say it on my newsletter, with a bit of a wink. At work I'd say let's use the time saved to get more video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine. My job relies on being out at the scene, and my newsletter is growing by about twenty paying readers a month. The site's owners are making money from video adverts, so I'm not worried about cuts in this version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and push the newsletter to five hundred paying readers by the end of next year, with a local sponsor, maybe the garden centre. I'd keep using AI to draft alerts so I can spend more time filming. I'd put the newsletter money straight into savings, so we'd have closer to six months by next winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Busy and calm. This is basically my life now, just carrying on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who panicked wasted energy. Is anyone at the site panicking now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, on the night desk, thinks AI will take everything and hasn't learned a single tool. I like Dev a lot, but he's refused to even try them. Dev (the night editor) would probably be the one person I'd worry for, even in this quiet version, because the routine overnight rewrites are what the tools do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk you'd still carry in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ad money is fickle, and that's why I built the newsletter in the first place. If a big advertiser pulls out, the site cuts, and that's been true since I started.

say: People who **panicked** wasted a lot of energy.
At work, the **time saved** should go into getting more video.
think: Her work depends on being **at the scene**, so she feels safe.
Her **newsletter** grows by about twenty paying readers a month.
do: Grow the newsletter to **five hundred** paying readers with a local sponsor.
Keep using AI to draft alerts and spend more time **filming**.
Bank newsletter income to reach about **six months** of savings.
feel: **Calm** and busy, carrying on with the life she already has.
S0.quote: Ad money is fickle, and that's why I built the newsletter in the first place.
fieldNote: She has already hedged with a **paid newsletter**, before any AI shock.
She leans on being **physically present** at scenes as her edge.
Her one worry is **Dev**, a colleague who refuses all tools.

steps.text: Keep covering crashes, fires and floods on video
Grow the valley newsletter to 500 paying readers with a garden-centre sponsor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, this is more like it. This is the one I've been preparing for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for local reporters to get back out of the office. I'd say it online and at work, and I'd probably run a little training video for other reporters on my newsletter. I wouldn't call for new rules, because I think the market will sort out who's worth paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the site will cut the desk-bound reporters and keep the ones who film. That's partly me, so I'm fairly safe, but it's not nothing. They'd probably also expect me to do the work of two people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask in January to lead the video side, with a small pay rise, since I'm the one doing it anyway. I'd buy a better camera and microphone, about eight hundred, from the newsletter money. I'd add a second paid product to the newsletter, a weekly planning and property roundup for the valley, because AI can help me read the applications fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a small worry for colleagues and for how tired I'd get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the market will sort out who's worth paying. What about colleagues it doesn't pick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel for them, I really would. But I think the answer is people learning new skills and churches and families helping out, not the government propping up a job that isn't needed. Dev (the night editor) could learn the tools in a month if he wanted to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Luke's business change anything for you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much in this one. Landscaping is hands-on, and robots spread slowly in this picture. If anything Luke's busier, because people with money to spare want their gardens done.

She reinvests side income in **equipment**, acting like a small business owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's sharp. I'd need a minute with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say local people will still want a face they know telling them what's happening on their street. I'd say it in a video, because that's the point. I'd tell other reporters to start their own thing now rather than wait for a redundancy letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the site lets almost everyone go by 2029, me included, because an AI can write and even voice a crash report the moment the alert comes in. Filming is the hands-on bit, and robots aren't due till 2031, but anyone with a phone can film, so that doesn't protect me much. My salary is most of our money, so losing it would really hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the newsletter now: push it to a thousand paying readers within a year, and start live events, like a monthly question night with the council leader in the church hall. I'd lean hard on AI tools to run it alone, with a weekend video round-up. Luke and I would put the house deposit on hold and keep every spare penny in cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but also sort of fired up. Like the night before an exam you've half revised for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Luke's work is hands-on. Does the robot timeline change the household picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a lot, actually. If his landscaping has until about 2031 before robots compete, Luke can carry the rent for a while if my salary goes in 2028. That gives me two or three years to make the newsletter pay a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI can write anything, why would people pay for your newsletter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they know me. My mum's in the choir, I went to school with half of them, and when I say the bridge is shut I've stood on it. I might be wrong about that, and I'd find out fast.

Reporters should **start their own thing** before the redundancy letter comes.
think: The site lets almost everyone go **by 2029**, her included.
Filming is hands-on, but **anyone with a phone** can film, so it barely protects her.

S2.quote: Filming is the hands-on bit, and robots aren't due till 2031, but anyone with a phone can film, so that doesn't protect me much.

Her bet is **trust** in a known **face**, and she admits it might be wrong.
She turns fear into action quickly, putting **family plans** on hold.

steps.text: Grow the newsletter to a thousand readers and run monthly church-hall question nights
Use AI tools to run the newsletter and a weekend video round-up alone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a real runway. I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for anyone who starts now, and I'd mean it. I'd probably run a free session for younger reporters on how to start a paid local newsletter. I'd be cheerful about it in public, maybe more cheerful than I feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the job at the site lasts maybe three more years and then shrinks fast. That's enough to make the newsletter my main income, but only if I keep growing it every month. The risk is that a dozen AI-run local newsletters appear in my valley and nobody can tell them apart from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and grow the newsletter to a thousand readers by 2029, then go full time. I'd register it as a small company with Luke as a director, so we can share the books and the van. We'd still buy a small house, but a year later than planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in charge. I can see the steps, and that helps a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be more cheerful in public than you feel. What's underneath?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Underneath is the worry that I'm a decent reporter who got lucky with a newsletter, and that luck doesn't scale. I've never run a company. Luke has, and he says the first two years are the hardest, and he wasn't competing with machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stand out from the AI-run newsletters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Live things, mostly. The question nights, a stall at the summer show, a video where I'm standing in the floodwater. And being honest about mistakes, which machines are oddly bad at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a lot of time to get ready, if you actually use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the easiest one to plan for and people have no excuse to be caught out. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it. I'd do a newsletter issue on what the valley's firms and schools should be doing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have built a proper little local media business by 2036, with events, video and a few paying sponsors. The site job would go at some point, but by then I don't think I'd need it. My real worry would be getting complacent with ten years in hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the site for three or four years, learning everything I can about selling adverts and running video. I'd grow the newsletter steadily and hire a part-time helper from the college by 2030. Luke and I would buy a house in the next two years and probably start a family around then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose, but mostly settled. This one feels like it rewards the people who already started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might get complacent. How would you stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself a hard target. If the newsletter and events don't pay at least half of my income by 2030, I'd change something, not just wait. Luke would hold me to it; he's stricter about numbers than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot date, around 2039, matter to you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For Luke, yes. His landscaping has until about 2039 in this one, so it's a solid second income for years. That's the household's safety net while I build mine.

fieldNote: She expects to have **replaced** the site job with her own business in time.
Her self-check is a **hard target** for 2030, enforced by Luke.
Luke's **hands-on** work until 2039 is the household's safety net.
Ten years brings back **family plans**: a house and children.

steps.text: Stay at the news site three or four years to learn ad sales

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my salary goes before my newsletter can pay a wage, and two years is very tight. What would help is local businesses advertising with local people they know, and churches and community halls letting us run events cheaply. I don't want a handout; I want customers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether readers will still care who wrote something. I'm betting my whole plan on yes. If people stop caring whether a human stood at the flood, I'm in trouble, and so is every local reporter in the country.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout; I want customers.
portrait: Grace is a **27-year-old** breaking news and video reporter for a commercial regional news site.
She uses AI **every day** to draft alert stories, and runs a paid **valley newsletter** on the side.
She lives with Luke, who runs a **landscaping business**, with about three months saved and church on Sundays.
She's calm in the quiet scenarios and turns every faster one into a push to **build her own business**.
She bets everything on readers caring about a **known face**, and admits that bet could fail.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her salary would go before the newsletter can pay a wage.
whatWouldHelp: Local firms **advertising** with reporters they know.
Churches and halls offering **cheap event space**.
